This Is How a Little-Known Chinese Hypercar Hit Over 312 MPH on a Public Road
45 photos
Photo: BYD
Lost in the avalanche of premieres coming our way from both the EICMA show in Italy and the SEMA gathering in the U.S., an exciting piece of news for the world of hypercars slipped through the cracks: somewhere in Abu Dhabi, a Chinese mechanical monstrosity set a few world records. This is the story of how that happened, starting from the end.
The Chinese car I am talking about is the U9 Xtreme , and it is the work of Yangwang, the luxury brand of Asian carmaking behemoth BYD. At the beginning of this month, the car and an army of engineers took to the Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road (E11), in Abu Dhabi’s Al Dhafra region, where it was caught on film hitting 312,65 mph (503.17 kph).
In doing so, the U9 Extreme is now officially recognized by the Guinness World Records and the FIA as the fastest production car in a single-direction run, and the fastest electric production car in a single-direction run.
There is no doubt in my head that you've probably heard about the achievement already, but it's probably worth taking a closer look at how the car came to be recognized as one of the fastest vehicles on the planet.
The U9 project has been in the news for just three years, after it was presented as a prototype back in 2023. And although the achievement in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the culmination of R&D performed on it over the past three years, it is not the car's only record so far.
Photo: BYD The first time it was driven fast enough for people to notice it was back in 2024, when it hit 192 mph (309 kph) at Wuhan Hannan Airport in China . Later that year, in October, the ATP Papenburg proving ground in Germany saw the car moving past at speeds of 243.5 mph (391.94 kph).
About one year later, the U9 was taken to the ATP grounds once more, where it managed to set the production car speed record of 308.33 mph (496.22 kph). The last pearl on this high-speed necklace, added at the end of last year, is the 6 minutes and 59 seconds time recorded on the Nurburgring Nordschleife, it too a record.
If you look closely, you can see that the previous high-speed runs of the car took place in specialized facilities. This November run, however, took place on a public road, and that came with a series of challenges for the engineers, the car itself, and the driver, Marc Basseng.
Local authorities had to close the road for two days, with a stretch of 6.2 miles (ten km) becoming unavailable for regular drivers during this time. Of that distance, the U9 had only 4.3 miles (seven km) available for its top speed run.
Photo: BYD This being a public road in the middle of the desert meant that special precautions had to be taken. Teams swept the tarmac, and then had to carefully inspect every inch of it to make sure not even things as small as wire particles from cleaning brushes were left on the ground.
Two warm-up runs were conducted on October 31, one day before the record-setting drive, and then engineers went to work trying to make sure that the battery and motor were in proper order. The warm-up also allowed the team to fine-tune the U9 before the official attempt.
Among these changes, the car's rear-wing angle was adjusted to provide the maximum levels of downforce on the rear axle, and the suspension software was modified to increase rebound damping so that the hypercar would better handle the tiny undulations in the road surface. Finally, the tire pressure in the Giti rubber was fine-tuned.
The record registered at the beginning of this month in Abu Dhabi is the result of engineering work that, according to the Chinese, makes the U9 Extreme a car of many firsts. The motors on each corner spin, for instance, at insane speeds of 30,000 rpm. This achievement was made possible, in part, by using the world’s thinnest super-silicon steel on the stator – just 0.1 mm.
Photo: BYD Combined, the four motors on the U9 Extreme put around 3,000 horsepower to the road, more than double the punch of the regular U9. On top of that, the quad-motor independent torque-vectoring system makes sure torque is adjusted at each wheel more than 100 times per second, making sure there is no wheel slip or loss of traction.
Such high speeds and power numbers also require the proper thermal management of the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) Blade battery, and that was achieved on the Extreme with the fitting of a 1200V platform, as opposed to the standard U9, which uses an 800V solution.
That also allowed for the increase of discharge rates to 30C, which are up ten times over those of a conventional battery, and about two times higher than in most other electric supercars . Yangwang says all of this means the battery can be discharged completely in just two minutes, but also that it can sustain extremely high current outputs without overheating or severe degradation.
Then, the U9 was fitted with track-focused semi-slick tires that minimized relative slippage between the rubber and the rim during hard acceleration or braking. Higher stability during extreme speeds and under higher lateral g in fast corners (something that didn't happen during the record run) is also achieved.
The record run in Abu Dhabi comes at a time when Yangwang is moving toward production scheduling for the U9 Extreme. We've already seen the first example, called Dawn Moment, at the Beijing Auto Show earlier this year, but we're not told how many more are in the pipeline in the near future. In all, the Chinese plans to roll out around 30 units of this beast. We're not told how much one of them could cost, but some are even talking about a value of close to $3 million.

This App Lets You Turn iPads Into CarPlay Head Units, Pull That Outdated Tablet From the Drawer
18 photos
Photo: @0xProbabillity on X
A new CarPlay project could breathe new life into your outdated iPad , as someone has created a way to run Apple’s projection system directly on the tablet.
This is done by transforming the iPad into a head unit, with an iPhone still playing the role of the brain powering the whole experience. You just need to connect your iPhone to your tablet and let the smartphone stream live data to the iPad.
While many people online are criticizing the developer for vibe-coding and point to similar other efforts that made the headlines in the past, the man behind this new effort says his effort is completely open-source and does not require jailbreaking.
On the other hand, such an application has low to almost zero chances of ever making its way to the App Store. While the beta testing - which the developer claims would open soon - would take place through TestFlight, it’ll certainly be interesting to follow this project and see how it unfolds in the long term.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution For now, it addresses one big shortcoming: once they no longer receive support, iPads are pretty much useless.
Once Apple stops shipping iPadOS updates to the tablet, it’s only a matter of time until app requirements are also upgraded to newer versions. This means that while iPads are still usable once Apple stops supporting them - so even if your iPad no longer gets OS updates, you can still use the installed apps - developers typically stop supporting these iOS versions shortly after that.
So the big question is what’s the oldest iPadOS version that this project supports. The developer doesn’t seem to have the full data, as he claims he just needs to wait for TestFlight data to figure this out.
If the app ends up running on outdated iPads, this is fantastic news for people who want to get CarPlay in their cars without spending any dollars. Many people are already using tablets in their cars specifically for apps like Google Maps and Spotify - I know, not everybody likes a gigantic screen in front of their eyes - while those who don’t want the tablet to be very intrusive have turned to custom dash builds with integrated iPads.
3D printing a custom dash to make room for an iPad or getting one online has become more common these days, and with this project, old tablets would finally have a new purpose, other than just being abandoned in a drawer.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution Your options to get CarPlay in your vehicle While this project is still in the works, your options to get CarPlay into an old vehicle where the manufacturer did not install a compatible head unit come down to just two options: the installation of an aftermarket receiver that supports the system out of the box or buying a dedicated CarPlay screen that can be installed on your dashboard.
The aftermarket head unit from the likes of Pioneer and Sony ( whose retirement from this business is imminent ) comes with one big advantage: it can be installed in place of your existing and outdated head unit, so it doesn’t eat up more space in the cabin. It can also show live footage from a parking camera.
The major shortcoming is that it requires professional installation, unless you're a DIY guy who doesn’t mind messing with cables and everything else. This service typically costs at least a couple hundred dollars, so the final cost of the upgrade is much higher.
CarPlay screens typically offer a plug-and-play approach and only need to be plugged either into the cigarette lighter socket or an USB port. Once they’re powered on, you can just connect your iPhone to the screen and start running CarPlay without further customizations.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The main shortcoming is that you’ll have a screen getting in the way, typically on the dashboard. If you already have a head unit that includes a screen, this means you’ll end up with two screens in your car, one for accessing vehicle functions and a secondary one for CarPlay.
The option that helps you avoid all of these and still get access to your apps is to run everything on your iPhone. If you pair the smartphone to your car via Bluetooth, you can have navigation app directions and music directly through the vehicle’s speakers. You only need to turn the iPhone screen on all the time for navigation in Google Maps and Waze.
An iPad, if it can still run Google Maps and Waze, can be a good replacement, though most people typically remove them from their cars when they arrive at home for obvious reasons. However, this wouldn’t be a genuine CarPlay experience, but still offer apps running on iPadOS, something you can already do on an iPad that continues to be supported. For the past 2 weeks I’ve been reverse-engineering how CarPlay actually works. Here’s my first working prototype CarPlay is running from my iPhone and streamed live to an iPad - no car, no wires, no hacks. Everything you see is real and running smoothly. The idea: turn any iPad/iPhone you already own into a modern, buttery-smooth CarPlay display for your car - no need to buy an expensive head unit. If you’d use this, drop a like/RT - if there’s interest I’ll keep building and open a beta soon. — 0xProbability (@0xProbabillity) November 4, 2026

Owner Paints His 1981 DeLorean DMC-12 in Electric Blue, Lists It for Sale
31 photos
Photo: Cars and Bids
Scrap everything you know about the DeLorean DMC-12, because it is no longer valid for this one car. DeLorean never sold a painted DMC-12, but the owner of this car took matters into his own hands and, after a frame-off restoration, it rolled out of the shop shining in blue.
John DeLorean conceived the DMC-12 as a wedge-shaped, futuristic-looking, unpainted stainless-steel supercar. He failed to meet the supercar requirements during development, but other than that, the DMC-12 checked all the right boxes.
Now, the owner of an early 1981 example has deleted the unpainted stainless steel part and brought a car finished in Electric Blue (paint code B5 Blue) into the spotlight with a gray leather interior and riding on 14-inch wheels up front and 15-inch wheels out back, wrapped in Hankook Kinergy ST tires.
The owner reconditioned and reinforced the frame, also applying a protective coating. The roof structure was upgraded to stainless steel, while most original lights were replaced by LEDs, with incandescent bulbs remaining in the headlights, instrument cluster, and A/C control panel.
Photo: Cars and Bids The front fascia was entirely reproduced in fiberglass with the lettering in stainless steel. The car got a DMC rear louver reinforcement bracket. A power-operated rear-mounted antenna and Drayton taillight circuit boards are also on the menu.
Pop those "oh, look at me!" gullwing doors and you have access to a completely overhauled cabin. The custom-wrapped steering wheel with contrasting blue stitching, matching the exterior paint, frames a speedometer scaled up to 140 mph (225 kph), because it was upgraded with a reproduction gauge during its restoration.
The truth is that the original factory speedometer on a North American DeLorean DMC-12 showed a maximum of 85 mph, with a secondary inner ring showing 140 kph. That poor speedometer has gone through much controversy.
Because the time machine in Back to the Future needed to hit 88 mph (142 kph) to activate its flux capacitor and travel through time, the filmmakers had to modify the gauge to read a top speed of 95 mph (153 kph) for the close-up shots, with the 88 mph mark clearly indicated.
Photo: Cars and Bids For the dashboard shots where the needle climbed to 88 mph, the crew didn't actually drive the car that fast. They manually pulled a cable attached to the back of the speedometer to make the needle sweep smoothly to the desired speed.
They also added the famous glowing digital speedometer box on the dash so the audience could easily read the exact numbers ticking up to 88 in bright red LEDs. But this car has none of that. It makes do with the upgraded 140-mph speedo.
A Saab mirror adjustment switch showed up on board, along with the custom shift boot with a custom parking brake and custom floor mats. The one selling the car has also come up with a Kenwood head unit with Bluetooth connectivity and a USB charging port with a voltage monitor.
The most interesting part of the story is under the hood, where the DeLorean DMC-12 finally got what it deserved. Back in the mid-1970s, John DeLorean had several engine ideas, with the Comotor Wankel Rotary being the original plan. However, it just didn't work out in his favor.
Photo: Cars and Bids He also considered Ford's Cologne V6, but eventually deemed it too dated and unsophisticated for his exotic sports car . Citroen’s 2.0-liter inline-four was also on the list, but it eventually turned out to be too weak for the DMC-12.
DeLorean was running out of time and had to come up with something quickly. So he resorted to the PRV 2.85-liter V6, an all-aluminum engine jointly developed by Peugeot, Renault, and Volvo. Because Giorgetto Giugiaro had designed the car's interior around a smaller mid-mounted 4-cylinder, the bulkier V6 wouldn not fit behind the seats without sacrificing cabin space.
The power plant could put out 130 horsepower (132 metric horsepower) and 153 pound-feet (207 Newton meters) of torque, which failed to make it the sports car that John DeLorean originally wanted to build. However, now, all the mods take it one step further.
The DMC-12 got a carburetor conversion, custom intake manifold, mechanical engine-driven fuel pump, ignition-switched 12-volt power supply wired to an automatic choke, aftermarket fuel lines, fuel tank pickup unit, air and fuel filter.
Photo: Cars and Bids Upgraded radiator fans with an adjustable fan switch made their way under the hood, and a straight pipe replaced the catalytic converter. There is no dyno sheet to prove how much the setup makes, but it is probably safe to assume that it might be the setup that John DeLorean was hoping to get for his DMC-12 .
The car has traveled 42,577 miles (68,521 kilometers) in 45 years. Expectedly, after that much time on the road, the car is far from perfect. There are chips on the front fascia and inside the rear corner of the doors, along with some paint touch-ups near the passenger door handle, the listing reveals.
A crack in the windshield, uneven trim along the inner windshield edges, and scratches in the driver- and passenger-side door glass, along with some rust on the engine bay and underbody components are also issues that accompany the car.
The seller reports that there is also an oil leak from the rear main seal, while the onboard clock and the instrument light dimmer are not operative. The future owner will also have to get a new spare tire, because the current one, sitting in the trunk, no longer holds air.
Photo: Cars and Bids The future owner will get the restored 1981 DeLorean DMC-12 with six keys (come on, who has six keys?) and two fobs, the window sticker, that spare that doesn't hold air, the jack and tool kit, along with the reproduction registration card.
The 45-year-old gullwing coupe has just been listed for sale on Cars and Bids. With six days to go, the highest bid reached $5,500, which is light-years away from the average price this model usually goes for: between $54,000 and $64,000 USD, depending on condition, mileage , and transmission, with the five-speed manual, like this car comes with, usually commanding more than the three-speed auto box.

2026 SEMA Show • Toyota Brings Fresh Adventure-Ready Concepts at the 2026 SEMA Show Under the Woodland Banner
Mitsubishi Lancer Drags Lamborghini Huracan, and Someone Was Clearly Sleeping at the Start Line
13 photos
Photo: Wheels Plus / YouTube
A Mitsubishi , which usually costs in America between $24k and $43k for the current roster made up exclusively of crossovers and SUVs, doesn’t have much in common with a Lamborghini, right? After all, the latter typically costs about ten times more than your average Mitsubishi…
However, there are moments when the lines between a simple compact sedan and a high-performance wedge-shaped supercar are blurred, such as when they meet at the local quarter-mile dragstrip for a quick brawl. Here’s an eloquent example.
The videographer behind the ' Wheels Plus ' channel on YouTube usually dwells around The Strip at Las Vegas Motor Speedway or MRP, which is short for Mission Raceway Park, aka Thunder by the River, from British Columbia, Canada, but on this particular occasion they are prepared to show us something from BMP.
That’s Bradenton Motorsports Park in Florida, of course, where they caught some cool rides at the FL2K event, including a Mitsubishi Lancer and a Lamborghini Huracan. The Italian-built supercar is a stylish-looking gray and orange-trimmed supercar packing contemporary Y-spoke chrome alloy wheels and orange-painted brake calipers. It doesn’t look too modified, though it does pack a chute strapped to its back, signaling that it means business.
In the other lane, meanwhile, resides the ‘shell’ of a former Mitsubishi Lancer, most likely the eighth generation – potentially even a Lancer Evolution VII. However, the Mitsubishi is barely recognizable now due to all the track-focused modifications. So, this should be interesting – on one side is an elegant V10-powered Lamborghini Huracan and in the other lane is a fully custom Mitsubishi Lancer brawler.
As it turns out, while we expected a big and feisty skirmish, the driver of the Lamborghini sizzled out – either the Huracan had a launch problem, or the driver was sleeping on the line. Either way, the Mitsubishi took off like a storm while the Lambo was still mustering its courage and controlled the race from start to finish, nailing a spectacular 8.15s pass at no less than 182 mph! Meanwhile, the Lambo could only do a 9.63s at 153 mph…
That’s a bit shameful, right? Well, anyway, both of these models are now extinct. The Mitsubishi Lancer isn’t in production anymore since early 2024, so there’s no trace of the mighty Evolution model either. The Lamborghini Huracan, meanwhile, was made from 2014 until 2024, too, but it received a successor – the all-new Temerario.
It’s a different ‘entry-level’ supercar altogether, as it’s now a mid-engine plug-in hybrid sports car featuring a 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 aided by three electric motors from the bigger V12-powered Revuelto, and it rocks no less than 907 horsepower in its base configuration. Alas, we have a feeling that many quarter-mile dragstrip enthusiasts will continue to rely on the Huracan due to its easily tunable V10 configuration, right?

Subaru Impreza WRX STI Comes Back to Life in a Bid to Entice Fantasy Land With Its Performance Look
8 photos
Photo: graziani_inspo / Instagram
In places like North America, the Japanese automaker Subaru continues to offer an extensive range of models, focused on both family-oriented crossovers and SUVs as well as classic passenger cars with a sporty flair. That’s a nice balance, right?
The Japanese automaker’s Subaru US division has on sale the 2026 Impreza compact five-door hatchback, the 2027 BRZ rear-wheel drive two-door sports car, and also the 2026 WRX compact sedan in the passenger car department. Meanwhile, the crossover SUV side of the business is much more developed nowadays.
Over there reside the 2027 Crosstrek compact CUV, the 2026 Forester, which battles with the former for the title of most popular nameplate, the mid-size 2027 Outback crossover which abandoned the high-riding station wagon style with the new iteration, plus the family-oriented 2027 Ascent three-row SUV. But that’s not all, since Subaru also has no less than three EV models: Uncharted, Solterra, and Trailseeker – all of them are SUVs.
Quite obviously, the passenger cars are massively outnumbered by the ICE, hybrid, and all-electric crossover SUV models – and now somebody aims to balance the situation while also putting Subaru in the position of reclaiming its fan base used to seeing an Impreza WRX STI in the lineup. So, meet this member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators who stopped dwelling across the parallel universes of vehicular CGI to make this vision a digital reality.
Lorenzo Graziani, a Torino, Italy-based virtual artist known as ' graziani_inspo ' on social media, has cooked up this unofficial, hypothetical Subaru design idea – he imagines the Subaru Impreza WRX STI back in action as a homologation special for a new WRC entry. By the way, the World Rally Championship is going through a massive transformation in 2027, aiming to lower costs and expand the grid by moving away from the overly complex regulations of previous years.
The new WRC27 cars and Rally2 models will be purpose-built and kit cars, respectively, instead of fully custom prototypes; the complex plug-in hybrid unit has been removed in favor of sustainable e-fuels, some of the components will be shared with the Rally2 class, and the top-tier car costs will be capped at roughly 30% of the previous-year financial burden.
As such, automakers have more leverage in developing their cars and at a fraction of the cost, allowing for additional ideas to enter the fray. Well, this pixel master thinks that it would be great to see Subaru back on the grid, and proposes this futuristic two-door coupe with slim LED headlights, a massive widebody design style, humongous round LED daytime running lights referencing the big lights used in motorsport for years, as well as a short rear adorned with a massive rear wing.
Inside, there’s a full roll cage and full bucket seats even for the homologation model, while the renderings also show us the competition model going back to WRC stages. Of course, this is merely wishful thinking, and the 2027 Impreza for the US , announced by Subaru of America late in September 2026, is vastly different.
The real 2027 Subaru Impreza has a new base trim level to make it the most affordable all-wheel-drive compact car in the United States with a starting MSRP of $24,595. It’s only offered as a five-door hatchback, but at least the more powerful 180-hp Subaru boxer 2.5-liter engine has become standard across the range. Honda makes just about everything with a motor, from lawnmowers and generators to cars, motorcycles, and even airplanes. Now the Japanese giant is adding another electrified vehicle to the list – a premium electric mountain bike.
Unveiled at EICMA 2026 in Milan, the new Honda RN0 marks the company’s first entry into the premium electric mountain bike market. And unlike many automotive-branded e-bikes that amount to little more than a licensing deal and a familiar logo slapped on someone else’s frame, Honda appears to have actually put some engineering muscle behind this one.
The RN0 was jointly developed with German high-end e-MTB manufacturer ROTWILD and features a proprietary carbon monocoque frame and distinctive gull-arm swingarm inspired by Honda’s motorcycle chassis development experience.
There’s actually some real history behind that connection. Honda experimented with mountain bike development in the early 2000s, culminating in its wild RN01 downhill racing bike. In 2005, that project won the overall series championship in the UCI Mountain Bike Downhill World Cup. Honda never turned the RN01 into a consumer bicycle, but more than two decades later, the RN0 is effectively picking up where the company previously left off.

The roughly 24 kg (53 lb) RN0 is set up as a multi-role electric mountain bike, featuring 160 mm FOX 36 FLOAT Factory Kashima front suspension paired with a FOX FLOAT X Factory Kashima rear shock. DT Swiss H1900 SPLINE wheels use a mullet setup with a 29-inch wheel up front and 27.5-inch wheel in the rear, while Shimano DEORE XT four-piston brakes handle stopping duties.
Those are some quality components, but the drivetrain may be even more interesting.
Honda is using Shimano’s new 2.3 kg drive unit, rated for up to 100 Nm of torque and 750 watts of maximum output, paired with a sizeable 720 Wh battery.
Shimano’s AUTO ASSIST can automatically vary motor assistance based on terrain and rider input, while AUTO SHIFT handles gear changes to maintain an appropriate cadence.
There’s even an Assist Carryover function that briefly continues providing power after pedaling stops, potentially making it easier to clear rocks, roots, and other technical obstacles that normally would see the assist grind to a halt right when it is needed most.
A 2.2-inch color display is integrated directly into the top tube, and there’s USB-C charging plus Shimano app connectivity for adjusting motor settings and electronically locking the bike.
Honda hasn’t yet announced pricing in its release, but with a carbon chassis, Factory-level FOX suspension, XT brakes, and premium Shimano electronics, don’t expect this to be the everyman’s electric bike.
If anything, the RN0 looks much more like Honda is finally bringing its motorcycle engineering mentality back to mountain bikes – this time with a battery and motor along for the ride.
